paras: The mobbing of George Jerome and expulsion of Black men from Howell, Indiana, took place on June 16, 1903, when white townsmen at Howell, near Evansville, forced a Black streetcar conductor off his car and that night beat three other Black men and drove them out of town at revolver point. No arrests were reported, and Southern editors took up the case as evidence of Northern hostility toward Black workers.

Howell was described as a railroad town of about 1,200 people with Louisville and Nashville shops, a few miles from Evansville on the Evansville street car line. An Evansville correspondent wrote that "for several years the sentiment against the negroes in Howell has been intense," and another dispatch mentioned "several attempts to rid the place of the race." During track repairs, passengers changed at the edge of town to a transfer car, and a Black man had been put in charge of it.

On the afternoon of June 16, by the Evansville accounts, a crowd of townsmen surrounded the car and made the conductor give way to a white man. The Evansville Courier said he made three trips before "a number of infuriated citizens" ordered him off and out of town, firing several shots "merely to frighten him." The citizens then ran the car to the edge of Evansville and gave it to a white conductor.

The New York Sun's Indianapolis special gave a harsher version: a dozen men boarded the car at night, beat conductor George Jerome "unmercifully" and ordered him never to run a car into the town again. It added that Jerome "was not accused of any offence" and that the company would employ no more Black conductors.

Late that night men patrolled the streets, and three Black men found in the railroad yards, sleeping in box cars according to the Courier, were set upon with "stones and sticks." According to the Journal, a "posse of citizens" beat them and forced them out of town at revolver point, so bruised they "could hardly walk"; their names were not learned. The townsmen declared that no Black person would remain, a telephone message promised "a warm reception" to any found in town, and the Sun reported that two Black families on the outskirts fled.
No report of arrests or prosecution appears in the coverage; the only response reported was the company's decision to hire no more Black conductors.

The Indianapolis Journal ran its Evansville special under "Howell Citizens Rage," opening "The color line was drawn at Howell," and the Evansville Courier's account reached a Kentucky weekly. The Sun's story, headed "Black Conductor Mobbed" over "Men of Howells, Ind., Drive All Negroes Out of Town," was reprinted nearly word for word in Richmond, in Augusta, Maine, in Mexico, Missouri, and in Westminster, Maryland, between June 20 and 27.

In the North, the Worcester Spy condemned the mob, saying the townspeople treated Black people "in much the way that mean and stupid boys sometimes treat stray curs." Southern papers made more of it: the Columbia Herald called it Indiana's "tip" to the South on the race question, and the Raleigh News and Observer said "Indiana folks, while brutal to negroes, are subservient to street car owners." The Vicksburg Herald called it "just hatred of the race," and the Fredericksburg Free Lance and Henderson Gold Leaf used the Sun's text to argue that the South was the Black worker's proper home.
The only Black-press notice found was one sentence in the Wisconsin Weekly Advocate on July 9, listing the attack among recent outrages and saying the mob "almost beat him to death."

The Sun, followed by the editorials and the Black weekly, described a night beating of the conductor by a dozen men. The earlier Evansville reports, closer to the scene, said only that citizens forced him off in the afternoon, the Courier adding that shots were fired to frighten rather than hit him. Evansville papers called the town Howell; the Sun called it Howells.

reader.title: Mobbing of George Jerome and expulsion of Black men from Howell, Indiana
bases: The conductor was made to leave his car and the town, three Black men were beaten and forced out of town at revolver point, townsmen declared no Black person would remain, and two Black families fled (A1, A2, A9).

Two Evansville-origin reports and the Evansville Courier (A1, A3, A9) and an independent Indianapolis special (A2) agree that white townsmen forced a Black conductor off his car and that night beat and drove out three other Black men; they differ on whether the conductor himself was beaten.

framing.detail: Indianapolis Journal: 'HOWELL CITIZENS RAGE / Black Man in Conductor's Uniform Excites Indignation', 'The color line was drawn at Howell'.
Sun headline 'BLACK CONDUCTOR MOBBED / Men of Howells, Ind., Drive All Negroes Out of Town', reprinted in Richmond, Augusta (Me.), Mexico (Mo.) and Westminster (Md.).
Worcester Spy editorial 'Colored Men Persecuted' mocked the mob's 'moral and physical superiority' and warned of outrages going unpunished.

Southern editors condemned the violence while using it to taunt the North and argue the South was the Black worker's home (Columbia Herald, Savannah, Raleigh, Vicksburg, Fredericksburg, Wilmington, Henderson).
Wisconsin Weekly Advocate listed it with an Indianapolis beating and the Belleville, Ill., burning as recent mob outrages.
